findings.title: Cleanup scheduler interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute for every cleanup job
findings.body: Changing the ticker from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1 makes the whole CleanUpService run all cleanup jobs ten times as often. This PR is about annotation deadlocks, and this change is neither mentioned nor justified. Because clean() is synchronous and has a 9-minute timeout, a 1-minute ticker will queue a tick while a long cleanup is running and then immediately start another run, so cleanup can execute back-to-back and increase database and CPU load. Revert to 10 minutes unless this operational change is deliberate and justified.

findings.title: Successful annotation cleanup batches are logged at Error level with the full ID list
findings.body: The new fetch/delete loop logs 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', and the equivalent orphan-tag messages via r.log.Error unconditionally, including when err is nil and when the batch is empty. The callback always runs once, so an idle cleanup still emits ERROR entries, and for large batches the ids value can contain thousands of IDs. This floods error logs and alerting and makes real failures hard to find. Normal progress should be logged at Debug, with Error reserved for actual failures; all new r.log.Error calls at lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579 need this treatment.

findings.title: High batch sizes can exceed MySQL/PostgreSQL bind-parameter limits
findings.body: deleteByIDs only special-cases SQLite. For MySQL/PostgreSQL it builds one ? placeholder per fetched ID (line 615), and those servers reject statements with more than 65535 bind parameters. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured above that limit, every batch DELETE fails with a parameter-count error and annotation cleanup stops; the previous single DELETE with a subquery had no such parameter limit. The code should also chunk or inline for non-SQLite dialects, or clamp the configured batch size.
